1407.7906_Q01.query: What is the primary purpose of target propagation as proposed in this paper, and how does it relate to back-propagation?
1407.7906_Q01.answer:
## Primary Purpose of Target Propagation

The primary purpose of target propagation in this paper is to perform **credit assignment across many layers of a deep network** by exploiting reconstruction as a *layer-local* training signal, thereby reducing the reliance on derivatives [Source 2]. Concretely, the proposal is to use auto-encoders (or conditional auto-encoders, whose "code" can depend on side information) to provide learned reconstructions that serve as **targets for intermediate layers** [Source 1].

The key insight is that a regularized auto-encoder tends to produce a reconstruction that is a *more likely* version of its input — effectively a small move in the direction of higher likelihood [Source 2]. When the auto-encoder takes both a representation of the input and the target (or any side information) as input, its reconstruction of the input representation provides a target pointing toward a representation that is more likely, conditioned on all the side information [Source 2]. Extending this down the hierarchy, each target $\hat{h}^l$ is an estimate produced by the upper layers of a value of the $l$-th level representation that is near $h^l$ and more likely than $h^l$, given the observed output $y$ [Source 5].

Beyond standard credit assignment, the approach is motivated by several additional goals:

- **Handling strong non-linearities:** Credit assignment through many levels of possibly strong non-linearities is difficult for back-propagation, and target propagation is designed to help in this regime [Source 2].
- **Discrete units:** By generalizing gradients, target propagation may allow training deep networks with discrete hidden units [Source 2].
- **Biological plausibility:** The authors hypothesize that such auto-encoder mediated target propagation could play, in brains, the role of credit assignment through many non-linear, noisy, and discrete transformations [Source 2].
- **Representation quality:** In addition to each layer being a good auto-encoder, the encoder learns to "please" the upper layers by transforming the data into a space that is easier for them to model — flattening manifolds and disentangling factors [Source 2].
- **Recurrent extension:** The framework generalizes to recurrent and recursive networks, where the past acts as side information, and reconstructions of past activations (based on present observations) become targets for improving those past activations [Source 3].

## Relationship to Back-propagation

Target propagation is best understood as a **generalization of back-propagation** rather than a replacement for it:

1. **Equivalent in the infinitesimal limit.** Back-propagation and target propagation are identical when the target is viewed as an infinitesimal direction of change and the gradient can be computed analytically [Source 1].

2. **Beyond infinitesimal changes.** Whereas back-propagation propagates gradients (infinitesimal changes), the deep auto-encoder decoding path generalizes gradient propagation in a *learned* way, allowing the method to handle not just infinitesimal changes but also larger, discrete changes [Source 2]. This is what potentially enables training with discrete-valued hidden units [Source 1].

3. **Learning the backward computation.** The authors explicitly frame the contribution as, "in a sense, proposing to learn the back-propagation computation," which both generalizes back-propagation (e.g., to discrete representations) and makes it more biologically plausible as a credit assignment mechanism for brains, including temporally recurrent ones [Source 1].

4. **Why the name fits.** Because each $\hat{h}^l$ estimates a nearby, more likely value of the layer-$l$ representation given $y$, the procedure is genuinely target-based — this is the sense in which it is related to back-propagation and deserves the name "target propagation" [Source 5].

Historically, target propagation traces back to LeCun (1986) and was previously proposed (Bengio et al., 1994) as a way to overcome optimization difficulties in training recurrent neural networks caused by long-term dependencies in sequential data [Source 1].

Abstract

We propose to exploit reconstruction as a layer-local training signal for deep learn- ing. Reconstructions can be propagated in a form of target propagation playing a role similar to back-propagation but helping to reduce the reliance on derivatives in order to perform credit assignment across many levels of possibly strong non- linearities (which is difﬁcult for back-propagation). A regularized auto-encoder tends produce a reconstruction that is a more likely version of its input, i.e., a small move in the direction of higher likelihood. By generalizing gradients, target propagation may also allow to train deep networks with discrete hidden units. If the auto-encoder takes both a representation of input and target (or of any side in- formation) in input, then its reconstruction of input representation provides a target towards a representation that is more likely, conditioned on all the side informa- tion. A deep auto-encoder decoding path generalizes gradient propagation in a learned way that can could thus handle not just inﬁnitesimal changes but larger, discrete changes, hopefully allowing credit assignment through a long chain of non-linear operations. In addition to each layer being a good auto-encoder, the encoder also learns to please the upper layers by transforming the data into a space where it is easier to model by them, ﬂattening manifolds and disentangling fac- tors. The motivations and theoretical justiﬁcations for this approach are laid down in this paper, along with conjectures that will have to be veriﬁed either mathe- matically or experimentally, including a hypothesis stating that such auto-encoder mediated target propagation could play in brains the role of credit assignment through many non-linear, noisy and discrete transformations.

5 Target Propagation for Recurrent and Recursive Networks

The ideas introduced in the previous sections can be generalized to handle training of recurrent and recursive networks by target propagation. The basic idea is that the past can be seen as side information or context for the present and future, and we want the auto-encoding structure to model the joint of past, present and future. In turn, this allows reconstructions of past activations based on present observations to become targets for improving past activations.

There are two fundamental differences between the situation of a feedforward stack of layers that we have discussed up to now and the recurrent network case, which can be revealed by inspecting the unfolded graph of computation in the recurrent case and comparing to the computational graph of the stack of feedforward representations, and associating each “level” with a “time step”:

1. There are visible inputs (the sensory inputs that can be clamped) coming into each level, i.e., the representations computed at each time step.

2. The same parameters are used to map the representation at “level” t to “level” t + 1, and vice-versa.

We can apply exactly the same recipe that we have described up to now for a stack of feedforward representations, with these two modiﬁcations. In the forward direction we obtain a regular recurrent net computation. The backward direction is now associated with a reconstruction network, but it is also a recurrent network, and it is a recurrent network without inputs. We know that such recurrent networks without input tend to compute either a ﬁxed point or a Markov chain (the latter if noise is injected).

1407.7906_Q02.query: According to Equation (1), what is the joint distribution over x and h structured as in the generative model?
1407.7906_Q02.answer:
In the generative model described in the paper, the joint distribution $p(x, h)$ over the observed input $x$ and the latent layers $h = (h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_L)$ is structured as a **directed graphical model** in which the layers are generated top-down in a chain [Source 1]. The generative process proceeds from the topmost latent layer down to the input:

$$h_L \Rightarrow h_{L-1} \Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow h_2 \Rightarrow h_1 \Rightarrow x$$

That is, $h_L$ stochastically generates $h_{L-1}$, which in turn generates $h_{L-2}$, and so on, until $h_1$ generates the observed data $x$ [Source 1]. This top-down chain corresponds to the deep generative decoder $P(h)$, which is paired with a deep approximate inference encoder $Q(h \mid x)$ that runs in the opposite (bottom-up) direction [Source 2].

A key training objective for this model is that the joint distribution over $h$ and $x$ produced by the generative model $P$ should match the joint distribution produced by the recognition network $Q$ — which, when the layer-wise auto-encoder pairs are good at minimizing reconstruction error, can be reduced to matching the marginal distributions $P(H_i)$ and $Q(H_i)$ at each layer [Source 2]. This framework is grounded in the variational auto-encoder perspective, where the objective is a lower bound on the log-likelihood, and the upper auto-encoders' reconstructions serve as proposed targets that indicate directions of higher prior probability for the lower layers [Source 5].

1407.7906_Q03.query: In Figure 1, what three main actors are illustrated for an intermediate layer h in the generative model?
1407.7906_Q03.answer:
Figure 1 illustrates three main actors for any intermediate layer $h$ in the generative model:

1. **The top-level prior $P(h)$** — the generative model's prior over the latent representation $h$, which can be represented, for example, by a deep denoising auto-encoder [Source 2].

2. **The decoder $P(x|h)$** — the generative pathway that maps the latent representation $h$ to the observed data $x$ [Source 2].

3. **The encoder $Q(h|x)$** — the approximate inference (recognition) network that maps the observed data $x$ back to the latent representation $h$ [Source 2].

These components are depicted in the figure alongside the associated layers of a deep generative decoder paired with a deep approximate inference encoder, with the overall objective being that the joint distribution over $h$ and $x$ generated by $P$ matches the joint distribution generated by $Q$ [Source 1]. The figure also visually distinguishes the latent variable $h$, the generated samples, and the observed examples $x$ [Source 2].

The training criterion tying these actors together works as follows: the encoder and decoder must reconstruct $x$ well (the lower auto-encoding loop), while $P(h)$ must model well the transformation of data $x$ into $h$ through $Q(h|x)$, with the entropy of $Q(h|x)$ increased where possible. In other words, the upper auto-encoding loop should do a good job of modeling $h$ given $x$, and the encoder should produce samples that are easy for $P(h)$ to model [Source 2].

Another, very different and very interesting view of a deep generative model is offered in the recent work on adversarial generative networks (Goodfellow et al., 2014). In that case, randomness can be viewed as injected at the top level (possibly at lower layers too, but that is a choice of the designer), while the intermediate levels are considered to be purely deterministic and continuous transforma- tions. What could make learning in such networks difﬁcult is that one still has to assign credit (by backprop) to all the layers of a deep net. Another less well understood potential issue is that for each update step of the generator network, a discriminator network must be sufﬁciently re-optimized to continuously track the decision surface between examples generated by the model and training ex- amples. Finally, another potential issue (which can be seen as part of the optimization problem) is that if the generator concentrates on some modes of the data distribution, there is very little pressure to make it generate samples for the other modes (only for the rare generated samples that approach these other modes does the generator get a signal). However, a great innovation of the adversarial network is that it opens the door to deep generative models whose layers are trained in a globally coordinated way and in which the noise is injected at the top level, which we consider here to be very important features.

1407.7906_Q04.query: What are the three main approaches deep learning methods have historically relied on to propagate training signals across different levels of representation?
1407.7906_Q04.answer:
The paper states that deep learning methods have essentially relied on **three approaches** to propagate training signals across the different levels of representation [Source 1]. However, the retrieved context only includes the description of the **first** of these approaches:

1. **Greedy layer-wise pre-training** (Hinton et al., 2006; Bengio et al., 2007; Ranzato et al., 2007): in this approach, the lower levels are trained without being influenced by the upper levels. Each level only tries to find a better representation of the data as it sees it from the output of the previous level of representation. While this approach has proven very useful as an *initialization* for the second or third approach, its potential disadvantage is that, by itself, it does not provide any global coordination between the different levels [Source 1].

Introduction

Deep learning is an aspect of machine learning that regards the question of learning multiple levels of representation, associated with different levels of abstraction (Bengio, 2009). These representations are distributed (Hinton, 1989), meaning that at each level there are many variables or features, which together can take a very large number of conﬁgurations. Deep representations can be learned in a purely unsupervised way (sometimes with a generative procedure associated with the model), in a purely supervised way (e.g., a deep feedforward network), or in a semi-supervised way, e.g., with un- supervised pre-training (Hinton et al., 2006; Bengio et al., 2007; Ranzato et al., 2007). It is possible to build deep representations that capture the relationships between multiple modalities (Srivastava and Salakhutdinov, 2014) and to model sequential structure through recursive application (Bottou, 2011) of learned representation-to-representation transformations, e.g. with recurrent neural net- works (Sutskever, 2012) or recursive neural networks (Socher et al., 2011).

Deep learning methods have essentially relied on three approaches to propagate training signals across the different levels of representation:

9 Conclusions, Questions, Conjectures and Tests

In this paper we have proposed a radically different way of training deep networks in which credit assignment is mostly performed thanks to auto-encoders that provide and propagate targets through the reconstructions they compute. It could provide a biologically plausible alternative to backprop, while possibly avoiding some of backprop’s pitfalls when dealing with very deep and non-linear or even discrete non-differentiable computations.

This approach derives primarily from the observation that regularized auto-encoders provide in their reconstruction a value near their input that is also more probable under the implicit probability model that they learn, something that generalizes gradients, and can thus be used to propagate credit (targets) throughout a neural network.

This approach has ﬁrst been derived from a training criterion that tries to match the joint of data and latent representations when they are generated upward (from the data generating distribution and upward through the encoder) or downward (from the learned generative model, and going down through the decoders). This criterion is equivalent to the variational bound on likelihood that has previously been used for graphical models with latent variables.

This paper discusses how this idea can be applied to a wide variety of situations and architectures, from purely unsupervised and generative modeling to supervised, semi-supervised, multi-modal, structured output and sequential modeling.

1407.7906_Q05.query: How is the KL-divergence between Q and P decomposed in Equation (3) to better understand the objective of matching P(X, H) and Q(X, H)?
1407.7906_Q05.answer:
The decomposition begins by expressing the KL-divergence as an expectation of the log-ratio between the two joint distributions, taking $Q$ as the reference distribution — this ensures that the training pushes $P$ to put probability mass everywhere that $Q$ does, and especially wherever $Q(X)$ does [Source 1]. Formally, Equation (3) writes:

$$
KL(Q\|P) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,h)\sim Q(X,H)} \log \frac{Q(X,H)}{P(X,H)}
$$

This expectation over the joint $Q(X,H)$ can then be split into interpretable terms by separating the contributions of the observed variable $x$ and the latent variable $h$ [Source 5]:

$$
= \mathbb{E}_{x\sim Q(X)}\, \mathbb{E}_{h\sim Q(H\mid x)} \log P(x\mid h) \;+\; \mathbb{E}_{h\sim Q(H)} \log P(h) \;+\; \text{entropy terms of } Q \;(H(Q))
$$

In other words, the criterion naturally decomposes into:

1. **A reconstruction term** — the expected log-likelihood of the input $x$ under the decoder/generative path $P(x\mid h)$, averaged over samples $h \sim Q(H\mid x)$ drawn from the encoder's posterior [Source 5].
2. **A prior-matching term** — the expected log-prior $\log P(h)$ under the aggregated posterior $Q(H)$, which encourages the latent distribution induced by the encoder to agree with the prior $P(h)$ [Source 5].
3. **Entropy terms of $Q$** — the differential entropy $H(Q)$ of the approximate distribution, which accounts for the $\log Q(X,H)$ numerator in the log-ratio [Source 2, Source 5].

The intuition behind this decomposition is that matching the joint distributions $P(X,H)$ and $Q(X,H)$ — rather than only matching the marginals $P(X)$ and $Q(X)$ directly — allows the objective to be evaluated while avoiding the intractabilities that arise when latent variables are introduced explicitly [Source 1].

Moreover, this decomposition can be applied **layer by layer**: for each layer $h^l$ in the chain, the upper layers $(h^{l+1}, h^{l+2}, \dots)$ are treated as implicitly providing the prior $P(H^l)$, since they are trained to model $h^l \sim Q(H^l)$ through the samples they receive as training data. This yields a per-layer criterion $KL(Q^l \| P^l)$, giving each layer's encoder and decoder parameters their own training signal [Source 4]. In this scheme, each layer's encoder tries to transform its input distribution into one that is easier for the upper layers to match — effectively flattening curved manifolds, since a completely flat manifold could be modeled by a single linear auto-encoder (i.e., PCA) [Source 3].

1407.7906_Q06.answer:
Figure 2 illustrates a possible back-propagation-free implementation of the training procedure for the proposed deep generative auto-encoder architecture, using a variant of the **recirculation algorithm** to train a single-layer auto-encoder without back-prop [Source 1].

In the paper's overall framework, each of the $L$ layers parametrizes an encoder $f_l$ and a decoder $g_l$, and the training objective requires that (1) each layer act as a good layer-wise denoising auto-encoder, (2) every "long loop" going up from $h_l$ and back down to $\hat{h}_l$ also functions as a good denoising auto-encoder, (3) each encoder produce output close to the reconstruction of the noise-free long-loop auto-encoder above it, and (4) each layer inject an appropriate amount of noise—just enough to make the decoder sufficiently contractive without excessively hurting reconstruction error [Source 1].

Figure 2, together with Algorithm 2, provides the concrete sketch of how this computation can be carried out without relying on back-propagation, i.e., by recirculating activations through the encoder–decoder loop so that the necessary credit assignment across layers is achieved by the auto-encoding/recirculation mechanism itself rather than by backpropagated gradients [Source 1].

Note that the retrieved context describes Figure 2 only at this level of detail (as the visual sketch accompanying Algorithm 2's back-prop-free recirculation scheme); the actual diagrammatic contents of the figure are not reproduced in the retrieved text beyond this reference [Source 1].

Introduction

Deep learning is an aspect of machine learning that regards the question of learning multiple levels of representation, associated with different levels of abstraction (Bengio, 2009). These representations are distributed (Hinton, 1989), meaning that at each level there are many variables or features, which together can take a very large number of conﬁgurations. Deep representations can be learned in a purely unsupervised way (sometimes with a generative procedure associated with the model), in a purely supervised way (e.g., a deep feedforward network), or in a semi-supervised way, e.g., with un- supervised pre-training (Hinton et al., 2006; Bengio et al., 2007; Ranzato et al., 2007). It is possible to build deep representations that capture the relationships between multiple modalities (Srivastava and Salakhutdinov, 2014) and to model sequential structure through recursive application (Bottou, 2011) of learned representation-to-representation transformations, e.g. with recurrent neural net- works (Sutskever, 2012) or recursive neural networks (Socher et al., 2011).

Deep learning methods have essentially relied on three approaches to propagate training signals across the different levels of representation:

1

1. Greedy layer-wise pre-training (Hinton et al., 2006; Bengio et al., 2007; Ranzato et al., 2007): the lower levels are trained without being inﬂuenced by the upper levels, each only trying to ﬁnd a better representation of the data as they see it from the output of the previous level of representation. Although this approach has been found very useful as an initializa- tion for the second or third approach, its potential disadvantage is that by itself it does not provide a global coordination between the different levels.

1407.7906_Q07.query: What is the main conjecture regarding the proposed training scheme's ability to handle very deep non-linear networks compared to back-propagated gradients?
1407.7906_Q07.answer:
## The Main Conjecture

The central conjecture is that **by providing a training signal at each layer, the proposed target-propagation scheme will be less prone to the training difficulties encountered when training very deep non-linear networks with back-propagated gradients** [Source 2]. In other words, rather than relying on a single gradient signal that must flow backward through the entire network, the auto-encoder-based approach gives every layer its own local learning signal, which the authors believe makes deep training more robust [Source 2].

## Why This Conjecture Is Motivated

The motivation stems from known weaknesses of back-propagation:

- Gradients with respect to lower layers, which must pass through many non-linearities, appear less able to correctly train those layers—especially in deeper networks that must learn abstract concepts composed from simpler ones [Source 3]. This problem is particularly acute for very deep or recurrent networks involving the composition of many non-linear operations [Source 3].
- Back-propagation requires continuous features and derivatives, making credit assignment across many levels of strong non-linearity difficult [Source 4].

Target propagation addresses this by exploiting reconstruction as a **layer-local training signal**: a regularized auto-encoder produces a reconstruction that is a "more likely" version of its input, effectively generalizing gradients so that credit can be propagated through targets rather than derivatives [Source 4]. Because this learned propagation can handle not just infinitesimal changes but larger, discrete changes, it may allow credit assignment through long chains of non-linear operations [Source 4].

## Important Caveats

The authors acknowledge two nuances to the conjecture [Source 2]:

1. **Back-propagation may still converge faster in some cases**: Back-propagating all the way through the network might still help Algorithms 1 and 2 converge faster to a good model of the raw data $x$.
2. **Supervised settings may favor back-propagation**: The advantage of back-propagation through layers is expected to be greater in the supervised scenario (Algorithm 5), where the full gradient chain carries more useful information [Source 2].

## Broader Implication

If the conjecture holds, this approach could serve as a biologically plausible alternative to back-propagation while avoiding some of its pitfalls when dealing with very deep, highly non-linear, or even discrete non-differentiable computations [Source 1]. The authors frame this as a hypothesis that must be verified either mathematically or experimentally [Source 4].

9 Conclusions, Questions, Conjectures and Tests

In this paper we have proposed a radically different way of training deep networks in which credit assignment is mostly performed thanks to auto-encoders that provide and propagate targets through the reconstructions they compute. It could provide a biologically plausible alternative to backprop, while possibly avoiding some of backprop’s pitfalls when dealing with very deep and non-linear or even discrete non-differentiable computations.

This approach derives primarily from the observation that regularized auto-encoders provide in their reconstruction a value near their input that is also more probable under the implicit probability model that they learn, something that generalizes gradients, and can thus be used to propagate credit (targets) throughout a neural network.

This approach has ﬁrst been derived from a training criterion that tries to match the joint of data and latent representations when they are generated upward (from the data generating distribution and upward through the encoder) or downward (from the learned generative model, and going down through the decoders). This criterion is equivalent to the variational bound on likelihood that has previously been used for graphical models with latent variables.

This paper discusses how this idea can be applied to a wide variety of situations and architectures, from purely unsupervised and generative modeling to supervised, semi-supervised, multi-modal, structured output and sequential modeling.

Abstract

We propose to exploit reconstruction as a layer-local training signal for deep learn- ing. Reconstructions can be propagated in a form of target propagation playing a role similar to back-propagation but helping to reduce the reliance on derivatives in order to perform credit assignment across many levels of possibly strong non- linearities (which is difﬁcult for back-propagation). A regularized auto-encoder tends produce a reconstruction that is a more likely version of its input, i.e., a small move in the direction of higher likelihood. By generalizing gradients, target propagation may also allow to train deep networks with discrete hidden units. If the auto-encoder takes both a representation of input and target (or of any side in- formation) in input, then its reconstruction of input representation provides a target towards a representation that is more likely, conditioned on all the side informa- tion. A deep auto-encoder decoding path generalizes gradient propagation in a learned way that can could thus handle not just inﬁnitesimal changes but larger, discrete changes, hopefully allowing credit assignment through a long chain of non-linear operations. In addition to each layer being a good auto-encoder, the encoder also learns to please the upper layers by transforming the data into a space where it is easier to model by them, ﬂattening manifolds and disentangling fac- tors. The motivations and theoretical justiﬁcations for this approach are laid down in this paper, along with conjectures that will have to be veriﬁed either mathe- matically or experimentally, including a hypothesis stating that such auto-encoder mediated target propagation could play in brains the role of credit assignment through many non-linear, noisy and discrete transformations.

1407.7906_Q08.query: In the context of a deterministic encoder, as described by Equation (8), what condition must be met for the reconstruction log-likelihood to be totally minimized, as shown in Equation (9)?
1407.7906_Q08.answer:
In the deterministic-encoder setting, the reconstruction log-likelihood (the third term, a reconstruction negative log-likelihood) is totally minimized when the encoder and decoder together form what the authors call a **perfect auto-encoder** relative to the data-generating distribution $Q(X)$ [Source 1].

The precise condition is that the decoder exactly inverts the encoder for every input $x$ drawn from $Q(X)$:

$$\tilde{g}_l(\tilde{f}_l(x)) = x$$

That is, when $h_l$ is computed deterministically, the reconstruction is perfect — and hence the reconstruction log-likelihood is totally minimized — so long as this exact reconstruction identity holds for all $x$ [Source 1].

This condition can be satisfied hierarchically: $\tilde{f}_l$ will constitute a perfect auto-encoder if each of the layer-wise auto-encoders at the levels below $l$ is itself a perfect auto-encoder [Source 4]. In other words, perfect reconstruction at a given level is guaranteed by composing perfectly reconstructing auto-encoders in all the lower layers.

Intuitively, this works because when the encoder is deterministic, no entropy is forced upon the reconstruction distribution $P(X \mid h)$ — the decoder simply needs to be able to recover $x$ from $h_l$, which is possible as long as no two probable inputs under $Q(X)$ are mapped to the same code $h_l$ [Source 3].

1407.7906_Q09.query: According to Figure 3, how do auto-encoders allow good targets at level l to be propagated into good targets at level l-1?
1407.7906_Q09.answer:
According to the illustration in Figure 3, the key mechanism is that the decoder $g_l$ approximately inverts the encoder $f_l$ [Source 1].

The logic works as follows:

1. **A good target at level $l$:** Suppose $\hat{h}_l$ is a good target for $H_l$ in the neighborhood of the current activation $h_l$, meaning that it lowers the cost:

$$\text{cost}(H_l = \hat{h}_l) < \text{cost}(H_l = h_l)$$

[Source 1]

2. **Invertibility through the auto-encoder:** If the encoder and decoder are good inverses of each other in the neighborhood of the reconstruction $\hat{h}_l$ — that is, if applying the encoder to the decoder's output recovers the target,

$$f_l(g_l(\hat{h}_l)) \approx \hat{h}_l$$

— then this inverse mapping allows the target to be pushed down one level [Source 1].

3. **A good target at level $l-1$:** Under these conditions, the corresponding lower-level target $\hat{h}_{l-1}$ satisfies

$$\text{cost}(H_{l-1} = \hat{h}_{l-1}) < \text{cost}(H_{l-1} = h_{l-1})$$

so $\hat{h}_{l-1}$ is also a good target for $H_{l-1}$ [Source 1].

In other words, because the decoder can map the improved top-level target back down through the encoder's inverse, a change that is beneficial at level $l$ translates into a change that is equally beneficial at level $l-1$. This is the core observation that justifies using auto-encoders for credit assignment via target propagation: each layer's decoder serves as the (approximate) inverse needed to convert upper-layer targets into lower-layer targets [Source 1] [Source 4]. The paper further conjectures that providing such a training signal at every layer makes deep networks less prone to the training difficulties encountered with purely back-propagated gradients [Source 5].

1407.7906_Q10.query: What is the key insight from Alain and Bengio (2013) that allows for estimating a target ˆhl for a layer hl?
1407.7906_Q10.answer:
The key insight from Alain and Bengio (2013) is that **score matching via denoising** can be used to estimate targets. Specifically, when a very small quantity of noise is injected into the auto-encoder and the training criterion is squared error (with continuous $h_l$), the difference between the reconstruction $\hat{h}_l$ and the uncorrupted input $h_l$ is proportional to an estimator of the score function:

$$\frac{\partial \log Q(h_l)}{\partial h_l}$$

where $Q(H_l)$ denotes the "true" distribution of the data seen by the auto-encoder [Source 1].

This is powerful because it means the reconstruction $\hat{h}_l$ can serve as a **proxy for the direction of the gradient** $\frac{\partial \log P(h_l)}{\partial h_l}$, where $P(h_l)$ is the implicit probability model learned by the auto-encoder sitting on top of $h_l$ [Source 1].

In practical terms, this enables the target-estimation step in target propagation: given a current representation $h_l = \tilde{f}_l(x)$, one can specify a change that moves $h_l$ toward a nearby value $\hat{h}_l$ that has a **higher probability** under $P(H_l)$ (or simply return $\hat{h}_l = h_l$ if $h_l$ is already a mode) [Source 1]. In other words, the denoising reconstruction naturally points toward nearby, more probable configurations of the layer's representation, providing a way to compute targets without relying on standard backpropagation.

This result is also generalized in the supervised setting, where the top-level auto-encoder takes the label $y$ as an extra input, and the reconstruction difference can be used to derive discriminant targets for the upper layers [Source 2, Source 3].

1407.7906_Q11.query: In the supervised learning context, what is the discriminant target for hx_L-1, as given by Equation (18)?
1407.7906_Q11.answer:
In the supervised setting, the discriminant target for the penultimate layer representation $h_{L-1}$ is defined by Equation (18) as:

$$\text{discriminant target} = \hat{h}_{L-1}^{x} + h_{L-1} - \tilde{h}_{L-1}$$

Here, $\hat{h}_{L-1}^{x}$ denotes the reconstruction of $h_{L-1}$ produced by the top-level auto-encoder when the label $y$ is given as an extra input, while $\tilde{h}_{L-1}$ denotes the reconstruction obtained when $y$ is missing [Source 2, Source 3].

The intuition behind this construction is that the term $h_{L-1} - \tilde{h}_{L-1}$ effectively removes from the reconstruction target (computed with $y$ available) the component that would have been predicted had $y$ not been provided at all. In other words, the target isolates the part of the reconstruction that is specifically attributable to the label information, so that the training signal pushes the encoder $Q(h \mid x)$ toward representations that capture the conditional relationship of $y$ given $x$, rather than merely modeling the joint distribution of $x$ and $y$ [Source 2].

Once this discriminant target is formed at the top level, target propagation then proceeds as usual for the lower layers [Source 2]. Furthermore, one can balance the joint-modeling objective (capturing $P(X, Y)$) against this discriminant objective (capturing $P(Y \mid x)$) by introducing a weighting parameter $\alpha \in [0,1]$, which yields the hybrid target of Equation (19) [Source 2].

1407.7906_Q12.query: How does Figure 4 generalize the architecture for supervised training?
1407.7906_Q12.answer:
In Figure 4, the architecture is generalized to supervised training by introducing the label $y$ as an **extra input to the top-level auto-encoder** [Source 1].

Key aspects of this generalization:

1. **Label as an additional input**: The top-level encoder $f_{L-1}$ (referred to as $f_L$ in the notation) takes three arguments: the input representation at the penultimate level $h_{L-1}(x)$, the label $y$ (or a vector of all zeros if $y$ is missing), and a mask $m$ — a bit indicating whether $y$ is observed ($m = 1$) or missing ($m = 0$) [Source 1].

2. **Handling missingness**: When an input variable is continuous, missingness can be represented explicitly by a binary vector indicating which input is missing, similar to the approach in Uria et al. (2014) [Source 1].

3. **Supervised training signal via reconstruction**: The reconstruction $\hat{h}$ of $h$ when $y$ is given provides a supervised training signal for changing the encoder $Q(h|x)$. This signal can be made discriminant by also considering the reconstruction obtained when $y$ is missing [Source 1].

4. **Split decoder**: The decoder $g_L$ takes $h_L$ as input and predicts $h_{L-1}$. It is split into two parts: $g_L^y$ for the part that predicts $y$, and $g_L^h$ for the part that predicts $h_{L-1}$ [Source 1]. When $y$ is a category (e.g., a one-hot vector), the $g_L^y$ part would use a softmax layer with cross-entropy (i.e., negative log-likelihood of $y$ given $h_L$) as the "reconstruction error" [Source 1].

5. **Prediction procedure**: At prediction time (Algorithm 4), the forward pass runs through the stack with $y$ missing — i.e., $h_L = f_L(h_{L-1}, 0, 0)$ — and the prediction is returned as $\hat{y} = g_L^y(h_L)$ [Source 2].

In essence, Figure 4 extends the unsupervised target propagation framework by treating the label as just another modality/input that can be either present or absent, allowing the same reconstruction-based machinery to provide supervised training signals.

1407.7906_Q13.query: What is a potential issue with sampling from denoising auto-encoders if the amount of corruption is either too small or too large?
1407.7906_Q13.answer:
When sampling from denoising auto-encoders, the amount of corruption injected during training creates a fundamental trade-off:

**If the corruption is too small:** the Markov chain mixes very slowly, meaning the sampling procedure takes a long time to explore the distribution properly [Source 1].

**If the corruption is too large:** the reconstruction distribution may no longer be well approximated by a unimodal reconstruction distribution, which is a key assumption in this framework since the decoder is treated as almost deterministic [Source 1]. This connects to a related problem discussed in the paper: with higher noise levels, the same corrupted configuration could be reached from many different training examples, causing the reconstruction to land "somewhere in the middle" — effectively filling the convex region between neighboring training examples with high probability values, which blurs the model's representation of the data manifold [Source 3].

**Potential remedies mentioned in the paper:**

1. **Sampling at higher levels of representation** — mixing tends to be much easier at higher levels of abstraction, so the generative procedure samples at the top level of the stacked auto-encoder [Source 1].

2. **Analytic sampling for special top-level structures** — if the top-level auto-encoder is linear (yielding a Gaussian prior) or element-wise (yielding a factorial distribution), sampling can be done analytically without requiring a Markov chain at all [Source 1]. The Gaussian case is particularly convenient because it affords a completely factorized representation with statistically independent factors [Source 2].

3. **Nearest-neighbor training procedures** — replacing the reconstruction criterion so that one only reconstructs toward a training set near neighbor, which helps avoid the blurring problem caused by excessive noise [Source 1, Source 3].
contexts:
However, as noted in Alain and Bengio (2013), one potential issue with sampling from denoising auto-encoders is that if the amount of corruption is small, then the chain mixes very slowly, and if it is large, then the reconstruction distribution might not be well approximated by a unimodal reconstruction distribution (which is what we are advocating here, since we assume that the decoder is almost deterministic). What may save the day, as argued in Bengio et al. (2013a) and Bengio et al. (2013b), is that mixing tends to be much easier when done at higher levels of representation. In the case of this paper, this is readily done by sampling at the top level, i.e., the generative procedure is summarized in Algorithm 3. In fact, if the top-level auto-encoder is linear, then its prior is a Gaussian one (see Section 7.1), and we can sample analytically, not requiring a Markov chain. Similarly, if the top-level auto-encoder is an element-wise auto-encoder (i.e., each dimension is auto-encoded separately), this really corresponds to a factorial distribution, and again we can sample analytically without requiring a Markov chain (see Section 7.2). Another interesting direction of investigation is to replace the reconstruction criterion of the penultimate level hL 1 by one in which one only tries to reconstruct to a training set near neighbor. This idea is expanded in Section 2.2.8 below.

Viewing the top-level auto-encoder as a Gaussian however has the advantage that one can replace the MCMC sampling scheme of general denoising auto-encoders by the analytic sampling scheme of a Gaussian. The auto-encoder weights can be mapped to the Gaussian covariance (and the biases to the mean) by a simple calculation. However, it is unlikely that every input distribution can be mapped to a Gaussian distribution, simply because we know that there are discrete factors typically involved (e.g., multiple disjoint manifolds). What really makes the Gaussian easy to sample, though, is that it affords a completely factorized representation, where the factors are statistically independent of each other.

The basic reason why a denoising auto-encoder learns to map its input to a nearby more probable conﬁguration is that it is trained to do so: it is trained with (input,target) pairs in which the input is a corrupted version of the target, and the target is a training example. By deﬁnition, training ex- amples are supposed to have high probability in average (this is what maximum likelihood is trying to achieve), and a random move around a high probability conﬁguration is very likely to be a low probability conﬁguration. In the maximum likelihood setup, we are trying to force the model to put a high probability on the examples and a small probability everywhere else. This is also what is go- ing on here: we are telling the auto-encoder that it should map points that are not training examples to a nearby training example. This mental picture also highlights two things: (1) the auto-encoder training criterion is more local than maximum likelihood (if the noise level is small, it only sees conﬁgurations in the neighborhood of the data), but higher noise levels should mitigate that, and (2) if we increase the noise level we will make the model do a better job at killing off spurious modes (conﬁgurations that are probable under the model but should not), however the model then might start fuzzying its reconstruction because the same corrupted conﬁguration could then be reached from many training examples, so the reconstruction would tend to be somewhere in the middle, thus ﬁlling the convex between neighboring training examples with high probability values. The latter observation suggests the nearest-neighbor training procedure sketched in Section 2.2.8 to avoid that problem. Another (orthogonal) solution to spurious modes, that was previously proposed (Bengio et al., 2013b) and works well, is the walk-back procedure: the injected noise is not completely ran- dom but along paths following reconstruction, i.e., we let the learner go from a training example towards a

Indeed, the auto-encoder only has limited representation resources (this is due to the regularization, contraction of the encoder and decoder functions) and in order to minimize reconstruction error it must use this capacity where it is really needed, i.e., to capture the variations in regions of high density of the data distribution, while ignoring variations not present in the data, by mapping unlikely input conﬁgurations towards nearby more likely conﬁgurations. Based on this intuition, we conjecture that the above result regarding the meaning of ˆhl − hl can be generalized to other settings, e.g., where hl is discrete or where a penalty other than the squared error is used to push ˆhl towards hl when training the auto-encoder. In support of this conjecture, there is the work on ratio matching (Hyv¨arinen, 2007), which generalizes score matching to models on binary vectors. Ratio matching constructs an energy function (an unnormalized probability model) model of the vector of input bits by relying only in its training criterion on the relative energy associated with the observed x and a “noisy” x obtained by ﬂipping one of the bits. It turns out that the ratio matching criterion can also be rewritten in a way similar to an auto-encoder reconstruction error (Eq. 3 of Dauphin and Bengio (2013)), with the i-th input being masked when reconstructing it (similarly to pseudo-likelihood). This is similar to the denoising auto-encoder but where the corruption noise consists in hiding only one of the bits at a time. This also suggests (although in a specialized setting) that the reconstruction probability associated to each input bit is “pointing” in the direction of a more probable value, given the input, but that remains to be proven in the general case.

1407.7906_Q14.query: In the context of a linear top-level auto-encoder, what is the form of the optimal denoising reconstruction function minus the input hL-1, and what does it behave similarly to?
1407.7906_Q14.answer:
## Optimal Denoising Reconstruction Function for a Linear Top-Level Auto-Encoder

When the top-level auto-encoder is linear and is trained to minimize the denoising reconstruction error, the optimal denoising reconstruction function minus the input $h_{L-1}$ behaves similarly to the **gradient of the log-likelihood of a multivariate Gaussian prior** $P(H_L)$ [Source 1]. This gradient takes the form:

$$\Sigma^{-1}(\mu - h_{L-1})$$

where $\mu$ is the mean and $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the Gaussian prior [Source 1].

### Key Behavioral Property

This gradient-like quantity **pushes the representation back towards the mean $\mu$ in a stronger way in directions of smaller eigenvalue** of the covariance matrix [Source 1]. In other words, directions along which the top-level representation has low variance receive a stronger corrective pull toward the mean.

### Numerical Stability Consideration

There is an important contrast with the true gradient in this setting:

- The **true gradient blows up** if some eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ are $0$, unless $h_{L-1}$ happens to already lie on the allowed manifold [Source 1].
- Even in that case, the result is **numerically unstable**, because it involves dividing a $0$ (the projection of $h_{L-1}$ onto the $0$-eigenvalue direction) by a $0$ (the eigenvalue with value $0$), and any slight perturbation of $h_{L-1}$ would throw this off [Source 1].
- By contrast, training the system as a **linear denoising auto-encoder yields a stable reconstruction**, because it always sees a numerically bounded reconstruction target and is trained with stochastic variations of $h_{L-1}$ [Source 1].

This is consistent with the broader observation in the paper that if the top-level auto-encoder is linear, its prior is a Gaussian one, which allows analytic sampling without requiring a Markov chain [Source 4].

1407.7906_Q15.query: What does Figure 5 illustrate regarding the architecture for structured output or multi-modal cases?
1407.7906_Q15.answer:
Figure 5 illustrates the architecture used for structured output and multi-modal learning, showing two modalities (here, $x$ and $y$) as an example. The key ideas are:

- **Separate representations per modality**: Each modality has its own representation, computed by its own stack of transformations — specifically, $x$ is mapped up to $\tilde{h}_1^x$ (with corresponding reconstructions like the generated or predicted $\hat{x}$), and $y$ is mapped up to $\tilde{h}_1^y$ (with the generated or predicted $\hat{y}$). The figure distinguishes between "observed" values and "generated (or predicted)" values, reflecting the generative setting where the model can reconstruct or produce samples in each modality [Source 1].

- **Top-level joint auto-encoder**: A top-level deep auto-encoder (at layer $L$) sits above the two modality-specific stacks and learns to represent the joint distribution $P(X, Y)$ — or a conditional distribution — over the two modalities. This top-level auto-encoder can then be used either for sampling (via MCMC) or for prediction (via MAP) of some modalities given others [Source 1].

- **Why the top-level auto-encoder must be deep**: Because the useful features of the joint distribution generally cannot be captured by the separate transformations of each modality alone, the top-level auto-encoder typically needs to be deep, with its own intermediate layers, rather than shallow. Shallow top-level auto-encoders are generally adequate for straightforward classification problems, but combining information from both $x$ and $y$ requires deeper structure — except in special cases such as when $y$ is an explicit one-hot representation [Source 1].

- **Generalization to $N$ modalities**: The same idea extends naturally beyond two modalities. For $N$ modalities $X^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(N)}$, each modality gets its own stack of auto-encoders that transforms its data $x^{(t)}$ into a representation $h^{(t)} = \tilde{f}^{(t)}(x^{(t)})$ such that the marginal $P(X^{(t)})$ can be easily captured through some $P(H^{(t)})$. A final deep stack of generative auto-encoders then models the joint representation formed from all the top-level hidden states $(h_L^{(1)}, \ldots, h_L^{(N)})$ [Source 2].

- **Directionality of inference**: The setup learned this way supports both directions of conditional modeling — if the architecture learns to represent $P(X, Y)$ and sample $P(Y \mid x)$, it can trivially be generalized to sample $P(X \mid y)$ in the reverse direction as well [Source 2].

9 Conclusions, Questions, Conjectures and Tests

In this paper we have proposed a radically different way of training deep networks in which credit assignment is mostly performed thanks to auto-encoders that provide and propagate targets through the reconstructions they compute. It could provide a biologically plausible alternative to backprop, while possibly avoiding some of backprop’s pitfalls when dealing with very deep and non-linear or even discrete non-differentiable computations.

This approach derives primarily from the observation that regularized auto-encoders provide in their reconstruction a value near their input that is also more probable under the implicit probability model that they learn, something that generalizes gradients, and can thus be used to propagate credit (targets) throughout a neural network.

This approach has ﬁrst been derived from a training criterion that tries to match the joint of data and latent representations when they are generated upward (from the data generating distribution and upward through the encoder) or downward (from the learned generative model, and going down through the decoders). This criterion is equivalent to the variational bound on likelihood that has previously been used for graphical models with latent variables.

This paper discusses how this idea can be applied to a wide variety of situations and architectures, from purely unsupervised and generative modeling to supervised, semi-supervised, multi-modal, structured output and sequential modeling.

3 Model Architecture

Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5, 2, 29]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations (x1,...,xn) to a sequence of continuous representations z = (z1,...,zn). Given z, the decoder then generates an output sequence (y1,...,ym) of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [9], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.

The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder, shown in the left and right halves of Figure 1, respectively.

1408.5882_Q01.query: What is the primary purpose of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the context of this paper?
1408.5882_Q01.answer:
In this paper, convolutional neural networks serve as sentence-level classifiers: they are trained on top of pre-trained word vectors to perform various sentence classification tasks, such as sentiment analysis and question classification [Source 1]. The core idea is that CNNs apply layers with convolving filters over the sequence of word vectors in a sentence, allowing the model to automatically extract relevant features from the input text for classification [Source 4].

The paper demonstrates that even a simple CNN architecture — a slight variant of the model by Collobert et al. (2011), with just one layer of convolution — achieves excellent results across multiple benchmarks with minimal hyperparameter tuning [Source 1] [Source 2]. The word vector for the $i$-th word in a sentence is represented as $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$, where $k$ is the dimensionality of the word vector [Source 4].

A key insight of the work is that the CNN acts as a strong classifier when paired with unsupervised pre-trained word vectors (from word2vec), and its performance can be further improved by fine-tuning the vectors to become task-specific [Source 1] [Source 2]. This supports the broader conclusion that unsupervised pre-training of word vectors is an important ingredient in deep learning for NLP [Source 2].

1408.5882_Q02.query: How does the paper describe the role of pre-trained word vectors in improving model performance, and what specific source was used for these vectors?
1408.5882_Q02.answer:
# Role of Pre-trained Word Vectors in the Model

## The Specific Source

The paper uses **word2vec vectors** trained by Mikolov et al. (2013) on **100 billion words from Google News**. These vectors have a dimensionality of 300 and were trained using the **continuous bag-of-words architecture**. They are publicly available [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3].

## How Pre-trained Vectors Improve Performance

The paper describes the role of pre-trained word vectors in several key ways:

1. **Compensating for limited supervised training data**: Initializing word vectors from an unsupervised neural language model is a popular method to improve performance when a large supervised training set is not available [Source 1].

2. **Serving as "universal" feature extractors**: The authors found that a simple CNN with one convolutional layer on top of these pre-trained vectors—despite little hyperparameter tuning—achieves excellent results on multiple benchmarks. This suggests the pre-trained vectors act as 'universal' feature extractors that can be utilized across various classification tasks [Source 2] [Source 3].

3. **Magnitude of improvement over random initialization**: The baseline model with randomly initialized words (CNN-rand) performs poorly on its own. While the authors expected gains from pre-trained vectors, they were surprised by how large the gains were—even a simple model with static vectors (CNN-static) performed remarkably well, competing with more sophisticated deep learning models that use complex pooling schemes or require parse trees [Source 4].

4. **Further gains through fine-tuning**: Learning task-specific vectors by fine-tuning the pre-trained vectors for each task (CNN-non-static) yields additional improvements beyond using them statically [Source 2] [Source 3] [Source 4].

5. **Combining static and task-specific vectors**: The paper also proposes a multichannel architecture that uses two sets of word vectors as separate 'channels', allowing the model to leverage both pre-trained (static) and task-specific (fine-tuned) vectors simultaneously [Source 2] [Source 3] [Source 5]. However, the results of this multichannel approach were mixed, and the authors note that further work on regularizing the fine-tuning process is warranted [Source 4].

Overall, the paper's central finding is that pre-trained word vectors provide a strong foundation for sentence-level classification, with the CNN models improving upon the state of the art on 4 out of 7 tasks, including sentiment analysis and question classification [Source 3].

1408.5882_Q03.query: What are the fixed hyperparameters used across all datasets for the CNN model, as determined by a grid search on the SST-2 dev set?
1408.5882_Q03.answer:
The CNN model in this work uses a single, fixed set of hyperparameters across all datasets, selected via a grid search on the SST-2 development set [Source 1]. These hyperparameters are:

- **Activation function:** Rectified linear units (ReLU) [Source 1]
- **Filter window sizes:** $h = 3, 4, 5$ [Source 1]
- **Feature maps:** 100 feature maps for each filter window size [Source 1]
- **Dropout rate:** $p = 0.5$ [Source 1]
- **$\ell_2$ constraint:** $s = 3$ [Source 1]
- **Mini-batch size:** 50 [Source 1]

Notably, the authors emphasize that they do not perform any dataset-specific tuning beyond these shared values — the only additional adaptation is early stopping on the dev sets (for datasets lacking a standard dev set, 10% of the training data is randomly held out for this purpose) [Source 1]. Training itself is carried out with stochastic gradient descent over shuffled mini-batches using the Adadelta update rule [Source 1].

This minimal tuning is a key point of the paper: despite using essentially the same configuration everywhere, the model achieves excellent results on multiple benchmarks, underscoring that the pre-trained word vectors — rather than elaborate hyperparameter optimization — are the main driver of performance [Source 3], [Source 5].

The results, however, are mixed, and fur- ther work on regularizing the ﬁne-tuning process is warranted. For instance, instead of using an additional channel for the non-static portion, one could maintain a single channel but employ extra dimensions that are allowed to be modiﬁed during training.

Yoon Kim New York University yhk255@nyu.edu

Abstract

We report on a series of experiments with convolutional neural networks (CNN) trained on top of pre-trained word vec- tors for sentence-level classiﬁcation tasks. We show that a simple CNN with lit- tle hyperparameter tuning and static vec- tors achieves excellent results on multi- ple benchmarks. Learning task-speciﬁc vectors through ﬁne-tuning offers further gains in performance. We additionally propose a simple modiﬁcation to the ar- chitecture to allow for the use of both task-speciﬁc and static vectors. The CNN models discussed herein improve upon the state of the art on 4 out of 7 tasks, which include sentiment analysis and question classiﬁcation.

4.3 Further Observations

We report on some further experiments and obser- vations:

Kalchbrenner et al.

(2014) report much worse results with a CNN that has essentially

the same architecture as our single channel model. For example, their Max-TDNN (Time Delay Neural Network) with randomly ini- tialized words obtains 37.4% on the SST-1 dataset, compared to 45.0% for our model. We attribute such discrepancy to our CNN having much more capacity (multiple ﬁlter widths and feature maps).

Dropout proved to be such a good regularizer that it was ﬁne to use a larger than necessary network and simply let dropout regularize it. Dropout consistently added 2%–4% relative performance.

When randomly initializing words not in word2vec, we obtained slight improve- ments by sampling each dimension from U[−a,a] where a was chosen such that the randomly initialized vectors have the same variance as the pre-trained ones. It would be interesting to see if employing more sophis- ticated methods to mirror the distribution of pre-trained vectors in the initialization pro- cess gives further improvements.

We brieﬂy experimented with another set of publicly available word vectors trained by (2011) on Wikipedia,8 and Collobert et al. found that word2vec gave far superior per- formance. It is not clear whether this is due to Mikolov et al. (2013)’s architecture or the 100 billion word Google News dataset.

Adadelta (Zeiler, 2012) gave similar results to Adagrad (Duchi et al., 2011) but required fewer epochs.

5 Conclusion

In the present work we have described a series of experiments with convolutional neural networks built on top of word2vec. Despite little tuning of hyperparameters, a simple CNN with one layer of convolution performs remarkably well. Our re- sults add to the well-established evidence that un- supervised pre-training of word vectors is an im- portant ingredient in deep learning for NLP.

1408.5882_Q04.query: What was observed regarding the effectiveness of dropout as a regularizer in the experiments?
1408.5882_Q04.answer:
In the experiments on sentence classification, dropout proved to be an exceptionally effective regularizer—so much so that the authors found it was fine to use a network that was larger than strictly necessary and simply rely on dropout to regularize it [Source 1]. In terms of measurable impact, dropout consistently added 2%–4% relative performance improvement [Source 1].

The specific dropout mechanism used in this work was applied to the penultimate layer, combined with a constraint on the $l_2$-norms of the weight vectors [Source 2]. During forward-backpropagation, a proportion $p$ of hidden units is randomly dropped out (set to zero) to prevent co-adaptation of hidden units [Source 2]. Formally, given the penultimate layer $z$, the output is computed as:

$$y = w \cdot (z \circ r) + b$$

where $\circ$ denotes element-wise multiplication and $r \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is a masking vector of Bernoulli random variables with probability $p$ of being 1, with gradients backpropagated only through the unmasked units [Source 4]. At test time, the learned weight vectors are scaled by $p$ (i.e., $\hat{w} = pw$) and used without dropout to score unseen sentences, while the $l_2$-norm constraint rescales $w$ to have $\|w\|_2 = s$ whenever $\|w\|_2 > s$ after a gradient descent step [Source 4].

For comparison, in the Transformer architecture, residual dropout was applied to the output of each sub-layer (before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized) as well as to the sums of the embeddings and positional encodings, with a rate of $P_{drop} = 0.1$ for the base model [Source 3].

1408.5882_Q05.query: According to Figure 1, what are the main sequential layers in the model architecture after the sentence representation?
1408.5882_Q05.answer:
The model in Figure 1 of the sentence classification paper processes a sentence through the following main stages after the sentence is represented as word vectors:

1. **Sentence representation via concatenation** – A sentence of length $n$ (padded where necessary) is represented as the concatenation of $k$-dimensional word vectors:

$$
x_{1:n} = x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus \dots \oplus x_n
$$

where $\oplus$ denotes the concatenation operator [Source 4]. The example in Figure 1 uses two channels: one channel with word vectors that remain static throughout training and another that is fine-tuned via backpropagation [Source 4].

2. **Convolutional layer** – Convolution filters $w \in \mathbb{R}^{hk}$ are applied over windows of $h$ words to produce new features. A feature $c_i$ is generated from a window of words $x_{i:i+h-1}$ [Source 4]. In the multichannel architecture shown in the figure, each filter is applied to both channels, and the results are added together to compute $c_i$ [Source 4].

3. **Max-over-time pooling** – After the convolution, a max-over-time pooling operation is applied to the resulting feature maps, as indicated in the figure [Source 4].

4. **Final classification layers** – The pooled features are then passed through the remaining layers (fully connected layer followed by softmax) to produce the classification output [Source 1].

It is worth noting that this overall design follows a slight variant of the CNN architecture of Collobert et al. (2011) [Source 1], where convolutional layers with convolving filters applied to the input are the core computational component [Source 1].

The main result of this work is the following. On the WMT’14 English to French translation task, we obtained a BLEU score of 34.81 by directly extracting translations from an ensemble of 5 deep LSTMs (with 384M parameters and 8,000 dimensionalstate each) using a simple left-to-right beam- search decoder. 4 Why Self-Attention

In this section we compare various aspects of self-attention layers to the recurrent and convolu- tional layers commonly used for mapping one variable-length sequence of symbol representations (x1,...,xn) to another sequence of equal length (z1,...,zn), with xi,zi ∈ Rd, such as a hidden layer in a typical sequence transduction encoder or decoder. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata.

One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required.

The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [11]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types.

As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d, which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [31] and byte-pair [25] representations. 1408.5882_Q06.query: How does Figure 1 illustrate the concept of 'two channels' for sentence representation?
1408.5882_Q06.answer:
Figure 1 illustrates the "two channels" concept by showing how the input sentence is represented as an $n \times k$ matrix with two parallel copies of the word embeddings, each serving a distinct purpose [Source 2].

**How the two channels work:**

1. **Static channel**: One channel contains pre-trained word vectors that are kept fixed (static) throughout training, so they are never updated by gradient descent [Source 1].

2. **Non-static (fine-tuned) channel**: The other channel contains a copy of the same pre-trained vectors, but this one is fine-tuned via backpropagation during training, allowing the embeddings to adapt to the specific classification task [Source 1].

**How the architecture processes them:**

- The convolutional layer applies multiple filters of different widths (e.g., window sizes $h$) over these channels to extract features [Source 2].
- In the multichannel architecture, each filter is applied to *both* channels simultaneously, and the results from the two channels are added together when computing the feature value $c_i$ in the convolution operation [Source 1].
- Apart from this dual-channel computation, the model is otherwise equivalent to the single-channel architecture [Source 1].

**Why this design matters:**

The figure's depiction of two channels reflects a key benefit of fine-tuning demonstrated in the paper: the non-static channel can learn task-specific adjustments to the embeddings. For example, in the pre-trained word2vec space, "good" is most similar to "bad" (since they are syntactically similar), but after fine-tuning on the SST-2 sentiment dataset, the learned vectors in the non-static channel no longer reflect this — instead, sentiment-relevant relationships (like "good" being closer to "nice") emerge [Source 3]. Fine-tuning also lets randomly initialized tokens not in the pre-trained vocabulary (such as punctuation) learn meaningful representations, e.g., learning that exclamation marks signal effusive expressions and commas are conjunctive [Source 3].

In short, Figure 1 visually encodes the idea of maintaining two parallel embedding matrices for the same sentence — one frozen, one trainable — and shows the convolutional + max-over-time pooling pipeline operating over both [Source 1, Source 2].

1408.5882_Q08.query: Based on Figure 1, where is dropout applied in the model architecture?
1408.5882_Q08.answer:
In the model architecture of Figure 1 (Kim's CNN for sentence classification), dropout is applied to the **penultimate layer** — the layer of pooled features just before the final output (softmax) layer.

The mechanics work as follows: during forward propagation, for the output unit $y$, dropout uses a "masking" vector $r \in \mathbb{R}^m$ of Bernoulli random variables, where each entry is 1 with probability $p$:

$$y = w \cdot (z \circ r) + b$$

Here $z$ represents the activations of the penultimate layer, and $\circ$ denotes element-wise multiplication, so some units are randomly "dropped" (zeroed out) during training [Source 4]. Gradients are backpropagated only through the unmasked units [Source 4].

At test time, dropout is removed and instead the learned weight vectors are scaled by $p$ (i.e., $\hat{w} = pw$) when scoring unseen sentences [Source 4].

This regularization proved highly effective in this model: the authors report that dropout consistently added 2%–4% relative performance, and it acted as such a good regularizer that it was fine to use a larger-than-necessary network and let dropout handle regularization [Source 2].

4.3 Further Observations

We report on some further experiments and obser- vations:

Kalchbrenner et al.

(2014) report much worse results with a CNN that has essentially

the same architecture as our single channel model. For example, their Max-TDNN (Time Delay Neural Network) with randomly ini- tialized words obtains 37.4% on the SST-1 dataset, compared to 45.0% for our model. We attribute such discrepancy to our CNN having much more capacity (multiple ﬁlter widths and feature maps).

Dropout proved to be such a good regularizer that it was ﬁne to use a larger than necessary network and simply let dropout regularize it. Dropout consistently added 2%–4% relative performance.

When randomly initializing words not in word2vec, we obtained slight improve- ments by sampling each dimension from U[−a,a] where a was chosen such that the randomly initialized vectors have the same variance as the pre-trained ones. It would be interesting to see if employing more sophis- ticated methods to mirror the distribution of pre-trained vectors in the initialization pro- cess gives further improvements.

We brieﬂy experimented with another set of publicly available word vectors trained by (2011) on Wikipedia,8 and Collobert et al. found that word2vec gave far superior per- formance. It is not clear whether this is due to Mikolov et al. (2013)’s architecture or the 100 billion word Google News dataset.

Adadelta (Zeiler, 2012) gave similar results to Adagrad (Duchi et al., 2011) but required fewer epochs.

MPQA: Opinion polarity detection subtask of the MPQA dataset (Wiebe et al., 2005).7

3.1 Hyperparameters and Training

For all datasets we use: rectiﬁed linear units, ﬁlter windows (h) of 3, 4, 5 with 100 feature maps each, dropout rate (p) of 0.5, l2 constraint (s) of 3, and mini-batch size of 50. These values were chosen via a grid search on the SST-2 dev set.

We do not otherwise perform any dataset- speciﬁc tuning other than early stopping on dev sets. For datasets without a standard dev set we randomly select 10% of the training data as the dev set. Training is done through stochastic gra- dient descent over shufﬂed mini-batches with the Adadelta update rule (Zeiler, 2012).

1408.5882_Q10.query: Which of the CNN model variants achieved the highest accuracy on the SST-2 dataset, and what was that accuracy, according to Table 2?
1408.5882_Q10.answer:
According to Table 2, the **CNN-multichannel** variant achieved the highest accuracy on the SST-2 dataset, with a score of **88.1** [Source 2].

For comparison, the other model variants performed as follows on SST-2 [Source 2]:
- CNN-rand: 82.7
- CNN-static: 86.8
- CNN-non-static: 87.2
- CNN-multichannel: 88.1

This result is somewhat notable in light of the paper's discussion: the authors had initially hoped the multichannel architecture (which uses two sets of word vectors treated as separate channels) would prevent overfitting and outperform single-channel models, especially on smaller datasets, but they found the results across datasets to be mixed overall [Source 3]. On SST-2 specifically, however, the multichannel model did come out on top among the four variants.

4 Results and Discussion

Results of our models against other methods are listed in table 2. Our baseline model with all ran- domly initialized words (CNN-rand) does not per- form well on its own. While we had expected per- formance gains through the use of pre-trained vec- tors, we were surprised at the magnitude of the gains. Even a simple model with static vectors (CNN-static) performs remarkably well, giving

competitive results against the more sophisticated deep learning models that utilize complex pool- ing schemes (Kalchbrenner et al., 2014) or require parse trees to be computed beforehand (Socher et al., 2013). These results suggest that the pre- trained vectors are good, ‘universal’ feature ex- tractors and can be utilized across datasets. Fine- tuning the pre-trained vectors for each task gives still further improvements (CNN-non-static).

4.1 Multichannel vs. Single Channel Models

We had initially hoped that the multichannel ar- chitecture would prevent overﬁtting (by ensuring that the learned vectors do not deviate too far from the original values) and thus work better than the single channel model, especially on smaller datasets. The results, however, are mixed, and fur- ther work on regularizing the ﬁne-tuning process is warranted. For instance, instead of using an additional channel for the non-static portion, one could maintain a single channel but employ extra dimensions that are allowed to be modiﬁed during training.

4. The last term is the most interesting one, i.e., matching the marginals P(Hi) and Q(Hi). At any given layer l, it is doing two things, if we consider the pressure on Q and the pressure on P separately: (a) This marginal matching term is asking the upper layers to learn a prior P(Hl) that Q(Hl). This just means that the “input gives high probability to the samples hl ∼ data” hl ∼ Q(Hl) seen by the upper layers must be well modeled by them. For example, the upper layers prior could be represented by a deep denoising auto-encoder Q(Hl) as data. In that case we want hl to be the target for updating trained with hl ∼ the reconstruction of the auto-encoder. The input of that auto-encoder could be hl or a corrupted version of it. This is similar to what happens when we train a stack of auto-encoders or a stack of RBMs in the usual unsupervised pre-training way, i.e., where the data is propagated upwards by the lower layers and used as training data for the upper layers models (Hinton et al., 2006; Bengio et al., 2007). (b) The marginal matching term is also asking the lower layers to choose an invertible encoding ˜fl such that the transformation of Q(X) into Q(Hl) yields samples that have a high probability under the prior P(Hl). In other words, it is asking the lower layers to transform the data distribution (which may be very complicated, with many twists and turns) into an easy to model distribution (one that the upper layers can capture). Note however how the pressure on Q(Hl) (i.e., on ˜fl) and on P(Hl) are asymmetric. Whereas P(Hl) is simply trained to model the “data” hl ∼ Q(Hl) that it sees, ˜fl is pressured into producing samples more towards the modes of P(Hl), thus tending to make Q(Hl) more concentrated and ˜fl contractive. Overall there are thus two forces at play on ˜fl: to minimize the input space reconstruction error, it would like to spread out all of the x training examples as uniformly as possible across h- space. But an opposing force is at play,
